paper_a.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data (McMahan et al., 2016)

paper_b.title: Parallelized Stochastic Gradient Descent (Zinkevich et al., 2010)

metadata.description: FedAvg extends parallel/distributed SGD from the IID data-center setting to the federated setting with non-IID, unbalanced data on unreliable mobile devices. Algorithmically, FedAvg = local SGD with periodic averaging (same as Zinkevich et al. with multiple rounds). The key extensions are: handling non-IID data, partial client participation, and empirical validation that many local SGD steps work well even under data heterogeneity.

matches.explanation: Both define a distributed optimization problem over data split across $K$ workers/clients. The mathematical objective is the same weighted average of local losses: $f(w) = \sum_k \frac{n_k}{n} F_k(w)$. The critical difference: Zinkevich assumes IID data partitioning; FedAvg handles arbitrary non-IID distributions across clients.

FedSGD (one gradient step per round, then average) is closely related to Zinkevich's one-shot averaging. The difference: FedSGD averages gradients (not models) and does this every round (not just once). Zinkevich: one round of communication after all SGD steps. FedSGD: communication every step.

FedAvg with $E$ local epochs is a multi-round generalization of Zinkevich's parallel SGD. Zinkevich: each worker does $T$ SGD steps, average once at the end. FedAvg: each worker does $E$ epochs of SGD, average, repeat for multiple rounds. FedAvg interpolates between FedSGD ($E=1$, full batch) and one-shot averaging ($1$ round, many epochs).

Same local-SGD-then-average template. Zinkevich: run SGD independently, average final models. FedAvg: run SGD locally, send to server, server averages, broadcast, repeat. FedAvg adds: random client subsampling ($C$ fraction), weighted averaging by $n_k/n$, and multiple communication rounds.

Both discuss communication efficiency. Zinkevich: one-shot communication is maximally efficient. FedAvg: multiple rounds but reduces total rounds by 10-100x compared to per-step synchronization by increasing local computation ($E$ epochs between communications).

Directly related: Zinkevich assumes IID data and notes this is essential for the convergence guarantee. FedAvg's main contribution is demonstrating that local SGD + averaging works well even with highly non-IID data, which Zinkevich's theory does not cover.

The federated learning setting (privacy-sensitive data on mobile devices, unreliable connections, unbalanced data sizes) is the novel application context that motivates FedAvg. Zinkevich's setting is a standard data-center parallel computing environment.

FedAvg explicitly acknowledges the connection to local SGD / parallel SGD, noting that the algorithmic contribution is applying and validating the same idea in the much more challenging federated setting.
